<p class="mw-kicker">Marketing in 3 · <a href="../../2025/index.html">2025 in research</a> · No. 3 · Paper published 13 January 2025</p>
<figure class="mw-hero"><picture><source type="image/webp" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" srcset="../../images/web/2025-emoji-emotion-detection-960.webp 960w, ../../images/web/2025-emoji-emotion-detection-1600.webp 1600w"><img src="../../images/2025-emoji-emotion-detection.jpg" alt="Close-up of a screen full of yellow emoji faces, with a smiling face surrounded by small red hearts in sharp focus" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"></picture><figcaption>Every one of these faces is a label someone chose for their own feelings. Photo: Domingo Alvarez E on Unsplash.</figcaption></figure>
<section class="mw-answer" aria-label="Short answer"><h2>The short answer</h2><div class="mw-ans-grid"><p>They can, and more finely than a positive or negative score. Three marketing professors in Vienna trained a free tool, NADE, on about 110 million emoji-tagged posts. It reads any short text, predicts the emojis a person would attach, then converts those into eight emotions such as anger, fear, joy and trust. Against human judges it came closer than word-list tools, open-source AI classifiers and GPT-4.</p><div class="mw-ev" role="note" aria-label="Evidence level: 2 of 3 stars, several studies"><span class="ev-k">Evidence level</span><ol><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><i>★</i><i>★</i></span>One study</li><li class="on"><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><i>★</i></span>Several studies</li><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><b>★</b></span>Meta-analysis</li></ol></div></div></section>
<section class="mw-takeaways"><h2>Key takeaways</h2><ul><li>Nearly 70% of studies in top marketing journals that pull feelings out of text still settle for positive versus negative.</li><li>In 285,839 tweets about Nike&#x27;s Colin Kaepernick campaign, a standard tone score turned sharply negative, yet trust, joy and anticipation rose far more than any negative emotion.</li><li>Across 1.33 million YouTube videos, titles carrying fear, anger or anxiety went with more views, while joy, trust and anticipation went with fewer.</li><li>Word lists found anger, anxiety or sadness words in only about a third of those titles; the emoji route could score 88% to 95% of them.</li></ul></section>
<section id="what-the-researchers-did"><h2>What the researchers did</h2><p><a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1921-1978" title="Christian Hotz-Behofsits on ORCID">Christian Hotz-Behofsits</a>, <a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7220-9060" title="Nils Wlömert on ORCID">Nils Wlömert</a> and <a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7172-5592" title="Nadia Abou Nabout on ORCID">Nadia Abou Nabout</a>, all at WU Vienna University of Economics and Business, set out to
give marketers a cheap way to see which feelings sit behind customer comments. Most social listening dashboards label text as
good, bad or neutral. That hides a lot: an angry complaint and a sad one are both negative, yet they call for
different replies.</p><p>Their tool, NADE (Natural Affect DEtection), works in two steps. First it reads a sentence and ranks the emojis a writer would
most likely put next to it, whether or not the text contains any. Then it converts that emoji profile into intensity scores,
from zero to one, for eight basic emotions taken from a long-standing psychological model, plus 24 blends of them.</p><p>Because people tag their own posts with emojis, the training data label themselves. That removes the costly step of paying
people to annotate thousands of sentences, which is what holds most emotion classifiers back.</p>
<dl class="mw-facts"><div><dt>Training data</dt><dd>About 110 million single-sentence English posts with emojis, drawn from over 7 billion collected on Twitter</dd></div><div><dt>Emojis</dt><dd>151 faces, hearts and symbols from the standard &quot;Smileys &amp; Emotion&quot; set</dd></div><div><dt>Emotions</dt><dd>Anger, fear, sadness, disgust, joy, surprise, trust and anticipation, each scored 0 to 1</dd></div><div><dt>Benchmark</dt><dd>920 online workers rated 2,605 tweets about large US listed companies, about eight raters per tweet</dd></div><div><dt>Compared with</dt><dd>Two word-list tools (NRC and LIWC), four freely available AI models and GPT-4</dd></div><div><dt>Access</dt><dd>Free web app plus Python and R packages; runs on an ordinary laptop and keeps the data on it</dd></div></dl>
</section>
<section id="why-go-through-emojis-at-all"><h2>Why go through emojis at all</h2><p>Word-list tools score only the words in their dictionary, and social media is full of slang, typos and shorthand. In the
validation tweets, just 18% of the distinct words appeared in the leading emotion dictionary, and half the tweets contained no
dictionary word at all. Those tweets simply get no score.</p><p>Emojis sidestep the problem. A phrase like &quot;I&#x27;m tired of this lol&quot; has no entry in a dictionary, but the emojis people put next to
similar phrases do. The rarer emojis turned out to be the most telling: the faces that best separate mild annoyance from real anger
are outside the hundred most used. A tool that knows only the popular few would miss them.</p><p>There is also a practical gain. Unlike sending comments to a chatbot service, the scoring happens on the user&#x27;s own computer, so
customer messages never leave the company.</p>
</section>
<section id="how-close-it-came-to-human-judges"><h2>How close it came to human judges</h2><p>The team compared every tool with the average ratings of the human panel. NADE had the smallest errors on all eight emotions.
On a second measure, which checks whether a tool rises and falls with the humans across tweets, it also led everywhere except
surprise, where GPT-4 edged ahead.</p><p>Its typical error was about as large as the disagreement between two human raters, which is as good as such a score can
reasonably get. The other tools showed a telling habit: they called many tweets either flat or extreme and missed the moderate
middle where most real comments sit. The pattern held for tweets with and without emojis.</p>

<section id="three-tests-on-marketing-data"><h2>Three tests on marketing data</h2><p><strong>Brand tracking.</strong> The team pulled English tweets about Nike from the two weeks before and after its Colin Kaepernick campaign
began. A widely used tone score suggested a backlash. The emotion scores showed that much of the extra chatter expressed
confidence in and enthusiasm for the brand, a reading that would have changed how a brand team responded.</p><p><strong>Headlines.</strong> On the 3,966 channels studied, a general negative tone in a title looked good for views. Split into emotions, the
picture changed: high-energy negative feelings helped, while sadness and disgust made no difference. The authors suggest drafting
several titles, perhaps with a chatbot, scoring them and keeping the version the model predicts will draw most viewers.</p><p><strong>Demand forecasting.</strong> Star ratings say little when 63.6% of reviews give five stars. Using 6.6 million Amazon reviews of 5,000
books, the team forecast sales from ratings alone, then added emoji and emotion scores, other text tools, or both. The emoji scores
did most of the work, and NADE still improved forecasts that already used three established text tools.</p>

<section id="how-to-apply-it" class="mw-howto"><p class="mw-rsg-kicker">Marketing in 3 steps</p><h2>Ready. Set. Market.</h2><div class="mw-rsg"><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">1</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Ready</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Decide and prepare</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Pick one stream of short texts.</strong> Choose one place where customers write briefly, such as comments on your posts, product reviews or chat logs. Export the last three months into a spreadsheet, one message per row.</li><li><strong>Decide which emotions matter.</strong> Write down the two or three emotions that would change a decision. Anger matters to a complaints team; anticipation matters before a launch. Ignore the others for now.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">2</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Set</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Build it</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Score the messages on your own computer.</strong> Run the file through a free emotion scorer that works offline, so customer messages stay with you. Split long reviews into single sentences first and score each one.</li><li><strong>Check 50 by hand.</strong> Read 50 scored messages yourself, including some with jokes or sarcasm. If more than five look clearly wrong, use the scores as a rough guide rather than a verdict.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">3</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Market</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Launch and measure</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Watch emotions next to your mood score.</strong> Each week, chart your chosen emotions beside your usual positive and negative score. When a spike hits, check which emotion moved before you reply: anger needs a fix, worry needs reassurance.</li><li><strong>Test headlines against them.</strong> Write five versions of your next title or subject line and score each one. Put the two that differ most into a split test, and keep a running list of which emotions won.</li></ul></div></div></section>

<section id="what-to-expect"><h2>What to expect</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>A fuller reading of data you already have.</strong> The same comments start to show which feeling is behind a dip, not just that sentiment fell.</li><li><strong>Fast to start.</strong> No training data, no special hardware and no coding if you use the web app.</li><li><strong>Short texts work best.</strong> Posts, titles and single sentences score cleanly. Whole reviews blur into many weak signals unless you split them.</li><li><strong>Modest forecasting gains.</strong> Emotion scores add to what star ratings and other text tools already capture rather than replacing them.</li></ul></section>
<section id="where-it-does-not-work"><h2>Where it does not work</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>English out of the box.</strong> The app scores English text; other languages mean retraining the first step with the code.</li><li><strong>Trained on one platform&#x27;s users.</strong> If your customers use emojis differently from the people in the training data, compare a sample of scores with human readers before relying on them.</li><li><strong>Sarcasm and irony.</strong> A laughing face on a complaint, or a crying face on a joke, can flip the meaning and mislead any automatic score.</li><li><strong>Links, not proof.</strong> The YouTube and Amazon analyses show associations. They do not prove that changing a title&#x27;s emotion will raise views.</li><li><strong>Emoji habits shift.</strong> Meanings vary by age, culture and setting, and keyboard suggestions may make some emojis less informative over time.</li></ul></section>
<section id="questions"><h2>Questions marketers ask</h2><div class="mw-faq"><h3>What is NADE and is it free?</h3><p>NADE (Natural Affect DEtection) is a free emotion scorer with a web app and Python and R packages. It converts text into likely emojis and then into intensity scores for eight emotions and their combinations (Hotz-Behofsits, Wlömert &amp; Abou Nabout, 2026).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Is it more accurate than ChatGPT for emotion analysis?</h3><p>On this benchmark, yes for most measures. Scored against people&#x27;s ratings, GPT-4&#x27;s error for anger was almost half as large again as NADE&#x27;s, and NADE matched the human pattern better on seven of the eight emotions.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Why is sentiment analysis not enough?</h3><p>Feelings with the same sign do different jobs. Earlier studies the authors cite found angry reviews are judged less helpful than sad ones, and that fear and anger spread news further than sadness. A single positive or negative score cannot separate them.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Which emotions in a video title attract more views?</h3><p>Here, titles charged with high-energy negative feelings pulled in more viewers and warmer ones pulled in fewer, after allowing for each channel&#x27;s popularity month by month. It is an association across many channels, so test it on your own content.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Does customer data leave my computer when I use it?</h3><p>No. Once installed, the app does all its scoring on the device, which suits companies that cannot send customer text to outside AI services.</p></div></section>
<section id="also-new"><h2>Also new at the time</h2><div class="mw-also"><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing</em> · 2025</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/jrim-07-2024-0324">The role of creative strategies in enhancing consumer interaction with new product video advertising</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Niu, Ma, &amp; Niu</p><p>A content analysis of 757 video ads for new tech products from six companies found an inverted U: response rose as ads combined more creative strategies, then fell. The peak came at roughly three strategies per ad, for both small upgrades and genuinely new products. Ads for the most novel products drew weaker responses overall. Three well-chosen angles beat a crowded script.</p></article><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Psychology &amp; Marketing</em> · 2025</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/mar.22167">Is Virtual Reality Lonely? The VR–Isolation Stereotype and Its Impact on VR Adoption</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Slivkin, Elgaaied-Gambier, &amp; Hamdi-Kidar</p><p>Implicit association tests showed that people who do not own a headset link virtual reality with being alone, and that this image makes VR users seem less appealing to copy. The stereotype weakened when users were shown with other people in the same room, but not when they met others inside VR. Show the headset in a living room full of friends.</p></article></div></section>
